justification: SLC6A11 encodes GAT-3, and the literature provides extensive mechanistic support linking GABA transporter function to seizure control: altered GAT-3 expression in human epileptogenic (sclerotic) hippocampus (16456667), changes after kindling and kainate seizures in rats (9526043, 14620876, 15488295, 20851161), anticonvulsant effects of non-GAT-1 (GAT-3-preferring) uptake inhibitors (9255599, 14612144), and reviews implicating cortical GATs in epilepsy (15210304, 11241581). However, none of these demonstrate that sequence variants in SLC6A11 cause or associate with epilepsy in humans. The only human genetic studies involve a multigene 3p25 duplication with a non-epilepsy phenotype (16470700), an association with neuroleptic-induced tardive dyskinesia (18334916), and a candidate-gene pharmacogenetic study of vigabatrin-induced visual field constriction that failed replication (16675198) — an adverse drug effect, not epilepsy susceptibility. Therefore the evidence is biological/functional rather than genetic, placing this firmly in the Hypothesized category, with a small allowance for the human expression and tangential human genetic findings.

justification: No article reports pathogenic GABRG3 variants identified in epilepsy probands or families; there is therefore no basis for "Established". The strongest human genetic datum is the linkage study in childhood absence epilepsy (PMID 11904235), which gave negative LOD scores under homogeneity but a positive HLOD for the GABRA5/GABRB3/GABRG3 cluster at 15q11-q13; this is suggestive, region-level (not gene-specific) evidence and the authors explicitly state that association studies are still required. The Angelman syndrome work (PMID 12661934, 8146195) concerns multigene 15q11-q13 deletions encompassing three GABA-A subunit genes, so it cannot single out GABRG3, and the mouse data actually show that loss of the γ3 subunit alone produces no overt neurological phenotype. The remaining papers are about autism association (PMID 12092907), imprinting/methylation (PMID 17339270, 20631049), physical mapping (PMID 9126483, 10644429), or exercise behavior, and do not address epilepsy causation. Biological plausibility is high (GABA-A receptor subunit, inhibitory neurotransmission, epilepsy-rich 15q11-q13 locus), so "Hypothesized" best fits, with meaningful residual weight on "Existing" from the CAE linkage heterogeneity signal.

justification: The EPIGEN multicentre case-control study (PMID 17913586) in 2717 epilepsy cases and 1118 controls highlighted GABRR2 among five genes whose variation contributed to disease predisposition by set-association analysis, though the authors explicitly describe the association as tentative, population-specific, and in need of replication — this is a credible but non-definitive human genetic association, fitting "Existing". Biological plausibility is strong, since GABRR2 encodes the GABA receptor rho2 subunit (PMID 1315307) and GABAergic dysfunction is implicated in epileptogenic lesions and absence-seizure models (PMIDs 17267178, 12948615), which would otherwise support "Hypothesized". Other GABRR2 associations reported (alcohol dependence, autism, schizophrenia/bipolar, serum creatinine) are distinct phenotypes and do not directly strengthen the epilepsy link.

justification: Two primary human genetic studies report distinct pathogenic GABRA1 variants in independent patients: PMID 11992121 identified the Ala322Asp missense mutation segregating in a large French-Canadian family with autosomal dominant juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, and PMID 16718694 identified a de novo truncating GABRA1 mutation (975delC/S326fs328X) in a patient with childhood absence epilepsy, with functional loss of function. Several negative screens (PMIDs 14631097, 15955415, 8739126, 16256272) indicate GABRA1 mutations are rare rather than absent, which slightly tempers the strength of replication, hence some weight remains on "Existing".

justification: GRIK5 encodes the KA2 kainate receptor subunit, and the literature provides substantial biological—but not genetic—links to epilepsy: altered KA2 mRNA in hippocampi of temporal lobe epilepsy patients (PMID 9848088), changed KA-2 subunit expression after status epilepticus, kainate-induced seizures and repeated seizures in rodents (PMIDs 16819974, 11226670, 19154779, 16181416), and broader evidence that kainate receptor antagonism is anticonvulsant (PMID 12080343). No article reports epilepsy-associated variants in GRIK5; the only human genetic studies of GRIK5 concern schizophrenia (PMIDs 16325263, 19125103), bipolar disorder (PMID 19086053), and rapid-onset dystonia parkinsonism, where no mutations were found (PMID 15254951). Other genetic studies implicate GRIK2, not GRIK5 (PMID 7675232). Therefore the relationship is mechanistic/expression-based, fitting "Hypothesized," with a small allowance for "Existing" given the human TLE expression findings.

justification: All of the retrieved literature concerns CYP2C19 as a pharmacokinetic determinant of antiepileptic drug metabolism (phenytoin, phenobarbitone, clobazam/N-desmethylclobazam, stiripentol interactions) in patients who already have epilepsy; none reports CYP2C19 variants causing or predisposing to epilepsy itself. Human genotype–phenotype studies are solid but the measured phenotype is drug clearance, serum concentration, or drug toxicity (PMIDs 9333104, 9860067, 10805060, 15533655, 15569425, 20390258), which is a treatment-response trait rather than epilepsy susceptibility. The one study explicitly testing pharmacoresistance found associations with ABCC2, CYP2C8 and CYP2C9, not CYP2C19 (PMID 19415824), and the Ginkgo case report only suggests a mechanistic route by which altered CYP2C19 activity could lower anticonvulsant levels and permit seizures (PMID 16419414). Thus the evidence supports a biologically relevant, mechanistic (and at best drug-response-associated) link rather than a causal gene–disease relationship; no two independent studies demonstrate CYP2C19 variants causing epilepsy in probands or families, so Established is excluded.

justification: The only clinical genetic report (PMID 20111057) describes a 2.3-Mb 17p13.2p13.1 microdeletion encompassing at least 17 genes in a boy with intractable epilepsy; such a multigenic CNV cannot implicate GABARAP specifically, and the authors' own mutation screen of 142 patients with developmental delay with/without epilepsy found no pathogenic GABARAP variants, while the zebrafish knockdown produced craniofacial/head-size phenotypes rather than seizures. No human study reports a point variant in GABARAP causing or associating with epilepsy, so Established is excluded and Existing is only weakly supported by the deletion case. However, the biology is highly relevant: GABARAP traffics GABA(A) receptors to the plasma membrane, mediates inhibitory synaptic plasticity (rebound potentiation), and autoantibodies against it impair GABAergic transmission in stiff person syndrome, all mechanisms plausibly linked to seizure susceptibility (PMIDs 15601949, 17581952, 17581966, 16984900, 19034952). This profile fits Hypothesized: strong mechanistic/animal/in vitro rationale without human variant-level evidence.

justification: The only human genetic study of KCNA4 in epilepsy (PMID 18440780) sequenced KCNA4 in ADLTE probands and performed an association analysis of a non-synonymous KCNA4 variant, but found no segregating mutations and no modification of susceptibility — an explicitly negative result, so neither Established nor Existing is supported. justification: Several primary human studies report KCNA1 point mutations in independent families in which affected members have epilepsy/partial seizures in addition to episodic ataxia/myokymia: PMID 10355668 (Scottish EA1 family, novel KCNA1 missense, two affected with partial epilepsy, with functional dominant-negative data), PMID 11026449 (Family A, KCNA1 G724C, partial epilepsy and myokymia without ataxia, plus three other mutant families), PMID 19205071 (new family with a novel c.1222G>T p.V408L mutation in which all affected members have myokymia and epilepsy), PMID 20660867 (F414S family in which epilepsy complicates the EA1 phenotype), and PMID 10414318 (novel KCNA1 mutation in EA1 associated with epilepsy). PMID 11317272 adds a mother–son pair with KCNA1 G724C and epileptic seizures. Reviews (PMIDs 7620586, 11579435, 17575281, 16100538) restate the association as background and count only as citation, not evidence.

justification: No article reports CYP2A6 variants causing epilepsy in patients or families, so Established is excluded. The only human genetic study in epilepsy patients (PMID 20089352) genotyped CYP2A6*4 in 179 Chinese epilepsy subjects and found higher steady-state valproic acid concentrations — a pharmacogenetic/treatment-response association rather than a disease-susceptibility one, which best fits a limited "Existing" interpretation if drug handling in epilepsy is accepted as a relevant linked phenotype. Supporting biology is otherwise mechanistic/in vitro or animal: CYP2A6 is the principal enzyme metabolizing the antiepileptic losigamone (PMID 14704462) and hydroxylates the experimental AED MTMCD in human microsomes and recombinant enzymes (PMID 15066669), and CYP2A6 is noted as metabolizing valproic acid (PMID 15993850). The remaining articles concern nicotine metabolism, cancer risk, and allele discovery, with no epilepsy relevance. Hence probability is split mainly between Existing and Hypothesized, with a small residual for Novel since the single human study addresses drug levels, not epilepsy itself.

justification: The strongest evidence linking CACNG2 to epilepsy comes entirely from mouse models: the stargazer mutant (Cacng2 disruption) exhibits spike-wave absence seizures and ataxia, with allelic series, Cacng4 double mutants, GABA-A receptor changes, and AMPAR trafficking defects defining a plausible mechanism (PMIDs 9697694, 12925883, 15677329, 16914686, 18923036, 10515159). A rat model (GAERS) also shows increased corticothalamic stargazin expression as a candidate pro-epileptic change (18556211). In humans, however, the available studies are negative or exclusionary: CACNG2 was excluded as the SCA10 locus (10643919), excluded by linkage/sequencing in consanguineous families with childhood absence epilepsy (20561025), and no exonic mutations were found in a family with schizophrenia/epilepsy/hearing impairment (18322454). Human polymorphism associations exist only for chronic pain (20688780) and lithium response/bipolar expression (18408563), not epilepsy. Therefore the relationship is biologically well-supported but rests on animal models, i.e., Hypothesized.

The only epilepsy-relevant papers are a general review of glutamate receptors in epilepsy that merely lists mGlu6 among group III receptors (PMID 10515165), a mapping paper about the neighbouring mGluR4 gene and a juvenile myoclonic epilepsy locus (PMID 11223165, a different gene), and a rat audiogenic seizure study that explicitly found no change in mGlu6 mRNA while mGlu4/mGlu7 were upregulated (PMID 11432969) — effectively negative animal data. justification: The human genetic studies in this set are essentially negative: SCN2B screening in GEFS+/FS cohorts found no mutations (PMID 12011299), screening in core SMEI/SMEB found no SCN2B variants (PMID 14738421), and a large Chinese GTCS family showed no coding variants in SCN2B/SCN3B/SCN4B (PMID 20730464). Hence the relationship is best described as hypothesized, with residual weight for a weak/limited human association.

justification: Human mutation evidence clearly links RAB3GAP1 to Warburg Micro syndrome (PMID 15696165, 17351351, 20512159, 18286824), but none of these abstracts report seizures or epilepsy as a documented outcome in the probands, so no article demonstrates a direct causal link to epilepsy in its own results. However, the phenotype includes cortical dysplasia and a consistent pattern of frontoparietal polymicrogyria (PMID 20512159), and a review explicitly lists RAB3GAP1 among genes for bilateral polymicrogyria, a malformation syndrome whose hallmark clinical manifestation is epilepsy (PMID 19120042). Malformations of cortical development are a well-recognized structural cause/precursor of epilepsy, which supports the "Existing" category rather than "Established". The remaining literature is biochemical (Rab3-GAP catalysis, PMID 10859313) or concerns the paralogous RAB3GAP2 in Martsolf syndrome (PMID 16532399), providing mechanistic plausibility (neurotransmitter exocytosis) but not epilepsy-specific genetic evidence, hence substantial weight also on "Hypothesized".

justification: No article reports pathogenic CDK5 variants in epilepsy patients; the only mutation screen of CDK5 (PMID 17354000) was for motor neuron disease and found none, and CDKL5 mutation studies (PMID 20397747) concern a different gene. Human data are expression/immunohistochemical: deregulated cdk5/p25 in hippocampal sclerosis (16410749), abnormal cdk5 immunoreactivity in focal cortical dysplasia (12147310, 17441989), and elevated CDK5 protein in intractable epilepsy neocortex (19623530) — strong biological relevance but not genetic variant evidence. Strong supportive animal/in vitro work exists: p35 (CDK5R1) knockout mice with spontaneous seizures and aberrant hippocampal circuitry (11157084, 15483119), Cdk5 conditional knockouts with seizures and lowered seizure threshold (19948833, 19529798), PTZ kindling (20476644), and C. elegans convulsion susceptibility (16996038). This pattern — compelling mechanistic and model-organism data without human variant evidence — fits "Hypothesized," with a modest allowance for "Existing" based on human tissue findings (and a CDK5R1 polymorphism in one ganglioglioma patient, which is a different gene).

justification: All provided articles concern CLCN7 mutations in osteopetrosis (dominant ADO2, intermediate, and infantile malignant recessive forms); none reports epilepsy or seizures as an outcome measure, and no genetic association study with epilepsy is presented. The closest links are indirect: recessive CLCN7 (and OSTM1) mutations produce severe primary CNS involvement with neurodegeneration, cerebral atrophy, lysosomal storage and ceroid lipofuscin accumulation (PMIDs 14584882, 19904698, 19238435, 12662317, 16813530), a neurodegenerative/lysosomal phenotype of the kind often accompanied by seizures, and ClC-7 is a ubiquitous late-endosomal/lysosomal channel whose loss causes neurodegeneration in mice (PMID 11207362).
